1310.title: Forgiveness: pardon and overlook
1310.hook: a father swears to cut off the relative who slandered his daughter, and a verse asks him a question
1310.howItsDone: Islamic teaching on pardon draws on Qur'an 24:22 and the story of Abu Bakr resuming his support for Mistah, and on the hadith that Allah increases in honor a servant who pardons.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sidq, truthfulness, and the company of the truthful. Today, what to do when someone close has not been truthful at all, a story day four hundred ninety-six first told.

Abu Bakr had been supporting a poor relative, a man named Mistah. Then a false accusation spread through Medina about Abu Bakr's own daughter, 'A'ishah, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. And Mistah was one of those who repeated it. When the Qur'an cleared her name, Abu Bakr made an oath, in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: by Allah, I will never spend anything on Mistah again. On its face, a fair oath. A verse came down about it anyway.
screen: `ABU BAKR SUPPORTED MISTAH.` → `MISTAH SPREAD THE SLANDER.` → `AN OATH: NEVER AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The verse is in surah al-Nur. It speaks to people of means who swear off giving to their relatives and the needy. Then, in Pickthall's translation: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you? Allah is Forgiving, Merciful." Two verbs, in Arabic wal-ya'fu wal-yasfahu: pardon, and overlook. 'Afw is letting go of what you're owed: the debt, the punishment, the right to get even. Overlooking goes one step further: not raising it again, not keeping it ready for the next argument. Then the question. The verse doesn't argue that Mistah deserved help, or that the slander was small. It asks Abu Bakr about himself: do you want to be forgiven? His answer, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: yes, by Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me. And he went back to supporting Mistah, and said he would never stop. Notice the order. The wrong was named first; 'A'ishah's innocence was declared in the Qur'an itself. Pardon came after the truth, not instead of it. The hadith from the humility day, in Sahih Muslim, has a line for this too, in paraphrase: no servant pardons except that Allah increases him in honor. So 'afw isn't pretending. It's choosing, with the wrong fully seen, to let the debt go, and then to stop bringing it up.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who owes you something, an apology, money, a fairer word: not the deepest wound you carry, just something you can hold, and name the wrong plainly without shrinking it. Then hear the verse's question turned toward you, is there anything you hope to be forgiven for, and if you're ready, let one piece of the debt go, maybe not all of it. If you pray, you can say the verse's last words in your heart: Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.
'Afw. Pardon: letting go of what you're owed, with the wrong fully seen, and then overlooking it, not bringing it up again. Today's word.
Your line: pardon and overlook. The truth first, then the letting go. See you tomorrow.

1311.title: Gentleness in all things
1311.hook: a man relieves himself in the mosque, the crowd jumps up, and the Prophet asks for a bucket of water
1311.howItsDone: Islamic teaching on rifq draws on the hadith that Allah is gentle and loves gentleness in all things, and on the Prophet's gentle handling of the desert Arab in the mosque.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'afw, pardon after the truth, and then not bringing it up again. Today, the way a thing is done: softly, or hard.

A desert Arab walks into the mosque in Medina, goes to a corner, and starts to urinate. On the floor where people pray. The companions leap up, shouting at him to stop. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: leave him. When he's done, pour a bucket of water over the spot. You were sent to make things easy, not to make them hard. Today's word, rifq: gentleness.
screen: `A MAN IN THE MOSQUE CORNER.` → `THE COMPANIONS LEAP UP.` → `LEAVE HIM. BRING WATER.`

segments.voice: Look at what the Prophet was protecting. Not the man's behavior: the floor still had to be washed. In the version in Sahih Muslim, he called the man over afterward and explained, in paraphrase, that mosques aren't for this; they're for remembering Allah, for prayer and recitation. The lesson still got taught. What he protected was the man, from being chased off in shame, and the people, from turning harsh. Then the principle. 'A'ishah reports, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: Allah is gentle, and He loves gentleness in all things. Not in some things. In all of them: correcting someone, raising a child, arguing a point, cleaning up a mess. In Sahih Muslim she adds, in paraphrase: Allah gives for gentleness what He does not give for harshness. And: gentleness is not found in anything except that it beautifies it, and it is not taken out of anything except that it spoils it. The Qur'an says something close about the Prophet's own way with people. In surah Al 'Imran, in paraphrase: it was by mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them; if you had been harsh and hard of heart, they would have scattered from around you. So rifq isn't weakness, and it isn't letting things slide. The mess was cleaned. The rule was explained. Gentleness is the how, not a softer what.
screen: `THE FLOOR WASHED, THE MAN KEPT.` · `GENTLE IN ALL THINGS.` · `BEAUTIFIED OR SPOILED.` · `THE HOW, NOT A SOFTER WHAT.`

segments.voice: Unclench your hands if they're tight, and bring to mind one thing today that tends to come out hard: correcting someone at work, reminding a child for the third time, a text to someone who annoys you. Run it once in your mind the hard way, then again with rifq, the same message in a slower voice with a softer hand, and notice what changes. If you pray, you can ask Allah, who is gentle, for gentleness.
Rifq. Gentleness: the manner of doing anything, so that the truth still gets said and the mess still gets cleaned, without the harshness that spoils it. Today's word.
Your line: gentle in all things. Same message, softer hand. Go gently.

1312.title: Justice, nearest to taqwa
1312.hook: a thumb near the scale, and the verse that puts fairness next to mindfulness of Allah
1312.howItsDone: Muslims read al-Ma'idah 5:8 as tying justice to taqwa, and the hadith of the just on pulpits of light extends fairness to judgments, families and anything a person is put in charge of.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rifq, gentleness as the how, not a softer what. Today, a virtue that sounds hard-edged, and the surprising company the Qur'an keeps it in.

Grapes go on one side of a market scale, a weight on the other, and a thumb hovers just above the pan. Nobody is watching the thumb. That's the whole drama of fairness: much of it happens where no one is checking. Surah al-Ma'idah gives justice an unexpected neighbor. Not courage. Not law. In Pickthall's translation: "Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty."
screen: `A THUMB ABOVE THE PAN.` → `NOBODY IS CHECKING.` → `DEAL JUSTLY, THAT IS NEARER.`

segments.voice: Pickthall says duty. In the Arabic of the verse it's taqwa: mindfulness of Allah, guarding yourself, keeping watch over what you do. English struggles to hold it in one word, so translators choose different ones. And what comes nearest to it? Not a long night of prayer. Not a fast. Dealing justly. The word for justice is 'adl, and its picture is a balance: two sides level, nothing tipped. So taqwa isn't only something on a prayer mat. It shows up at the counter, in how a bill gets split, in how a fight gets retold. Second, the sky and the scale. Surah al-Rahman, in paraphrase: He raised the heaven and set up the balance, so do not cheat the balance; keep the weight fair and don't make the measure short. Third, the home. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, speaks of people on pulpits of light near Allah. In paraphrase: those who are just in their judgments, with their families, and in whatever they're put in charge of. The parent dividing the last slice. The older sister picking teams. The manager handing out the good shifts. And the same verse in al-Ma'idah won't let dislike off the hook: hatred of a people must not push anyone away from justice. Day six hundred seventy-seven gave that a day of its own. Today's focus is closer: fairness as a way of being mindful of Allah, right where the thumb is.
screen: `TAQWA: PICKTHALL SAYS DUTY.` · `'ADL: A BALANCE HELD LEVEL.` · `THE SKY AND THE SCALE TOGETHER.` · `PULPITS OF LIGHT: JUST AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you'll divide or decide today, time, chores, credit for a piece of work, the last of the food, and look at it like a scale: where's your thumb, and is your side quietly a little heavier? Level that one thing in your mind and see it sitting even. If you pray, you can hold the line from al-Ma'idah: deal justly, that is nearer to your duty.
Justice. 'Adl: a balance held level, at the market, at home and in judgment, and called in surah al-Ma'idah nearer to taqwa. Today's word.
Your line: nearest to taqwa. Fairness lives right where nobody is checking. Tomorrow, keeping the ties of kin.

1313.title: Keeping ties
1313.hook: a relative gone quiet, and a promise about provision and life
1313.howItsDone: Muslims treat silat al-rahim, keeping ties with relatives, as a religious duty: visiting, calling, helping and greeting family, and reaching out again after a falling-out.

segments.voice: Yesterday: justice, nearest to taqwa, with the thumb kept off the scale. Today, the people none of us chose; day six hundred eighty-three first tied the rahim to al-Rahman.

Somewhere in a phone there's a family name with no messages since last year. An aunt. A cousin. A brother, after something nobody brings up at dinner. Families drift without anyone deciding to let them. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, attaches a promise to exactly those names. In paraphrase: whoever would like his provision to be widened and his life to be lengthened, let him keep his ties of kinship.
screen: `A NAME WITH NO MESSAGES.` → `FAMILIES DRIFT.` → `WIDER PROVISION, LONGER LIFE.`

segments.voice: The phrase is silat al-rahim. Silah is a connection, a joining. Rahim is the womb, and through it everyone you're related to by birth. The opening verse of surah al-Nisa asks people, in paraphrase, to be mindful of Allah, and of the wombs, the kinship by which they ask things of one another. Then the name inside the word. In Bukhari, the Prophet says, in paraphrase: the rahim is a branch from al-Rahman, the Most Merciful. Whoever keeps it joined, Allah keeps joined to him; whoever cuts it, Allah cuts off. The word for family and the name of mercy share their letters, and the hadith turns that into a bond. Then the hard part, also in Bukhari, in paraphrase: the one who keeps ties isn't the one who simply repays in kind. It's the one who, when the tie has been cut, joins it again. Not the relative who calls back. The one who calls first, after the silence. In Sahih Muslim, a man complains: I keep ties with my relatives, and they cut me; I'm good to them, and they're bad to me. The answer, in paraphrase: if it's as you say, it's as if you're feeding them hot ashes, and a helper from Allah stays with you as long as you keep on. And a caution. Keeping ties doesn't require pretending harm never happened. What a tie looks like with a truly harmful relative is a question to bring to a scholar you trust. But the default the hadith sets is the open line.
screen: `SILAH: A JOINING. RAHIM: THE WOMB.` · `A BRANCH FROM AL-RAHMAN.` · `REJOIN WHAT WAS CUT.` · `HOT ASHES, AND A HELPER.`

segments.voice: Let one relative come to mind, someone you've let drift, not the hardest one, and see their face. Remember one good thing about them, a meal, a joke, a ride somewhere years ago, and picture the few small words you might send them. If you pray, you can make du'a for them by name.
Silat al-rahim. Keeping the ties of kinship, the rahim a hadith calls a branch from al-Rahman: joined again, even when someone else cut it. Today's word.
Your line: keep the ties. Rejoining counts most when the tie was cut. See you tomorrow.

1314.title: Loving for others
1314.hook: a friend's good news, a half-second pause, and a hadith that walks straight into it
1314.howItsDone: Muslims cite this hadith as a measure of faith: wanting for others the good one wants for oneself, and making du'a for others' good.

segments.voice: Yesterday: silat al-rahim, ties joined again even when someone else cut them. Today, a sentence about what you want, and who else you want it for.

A friend gets the job you both applied for. Or the apartment. Or the news you've waited years to hear yourself. The text arrives, and for some people there's a half-second before typing congratulations where something tightens. Nobody chooses that half-second. But a short hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari walks right into it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
screen: `THE FRIEND GETS THE JOB.` → `A HALF-SECOND PAUSE.` → `LOVE FOR HIM WHAT YOU LOVE.`

segments.voice: Look at how the sentence is built. It doesn't say: stop wanting good things. It starts from what a person already wants for himself: health, ease, being forgiven, a good name, rest. Your own wanting is the ruler. Whatever you'd be glad to receive, want it for someone else too. Then the verb. The hadith doesn't say give, or share, though those may follow. It says love: yuhibbu, he loves. It's about what the heart wants. You can't always hand someone what they need. You can always want it for them. Then who counts. The hadith in Bukhari says his brother. A narration in Sahih Muslim gives the same words with his brother, or, the narrator adds, his neighbor. And a narration in al-Nasa'i spells out what kind of thing is meant: of good. Not whatever you happen to crave, but the good: guidance, health, mercy, the thing that would actually help. And the strong opening: none of you believes. Some commentators read this as faith not yet complete, not as a person leaving Islam. The hadith points at a gap between believing in words and believing all the way down, and it finds that gap somewhere very ordinary: what happens inside when someone else gets the good thing. The half-second is where the hadith does its work.
screen: `YOUR OWN WANTING IS THE RULER.` · `YUHIBBU: LOVE, NOT ONLY GIVE.` · `BROTHER, NEIGHBOR: OF GOOD.` · `FAITH, ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you've been hoping for lately, rest, a good result, a door opening, and hold it a moment. Then bring someone to mind, maybe the one whose good news stung a little, and picture them receiving that same thing, staying with it until the wanting feels real, or at least a little closer. If you pray, you can ask for it for them by name, before you ask for yourself.
Loving for others. From the hadith in Bukhari: wanting for another person the good you want for yourself, as part of faith itself. Today's word.
Your line: love it for them. Your own wanting is the ruler. Tomorrow, contentment with little.

1315.title: Contentment with little
1315.hook: a full cart that never checks out, and a one-sentence definition of wealth
1315.howItsDone: Muslims cultivate qana'ah by thanking Allah for what they have, saying ma sha' Allah over good things, and following the hadith's advice to look at those with less rather than those with more.

segments.voice: Yesterday: loving for others, with your own wanting as the ruler. Today, a different kind of being rich.

An online cart, full, never checked out. A closet with the tags still on. A search at three in the morning for something nobody needed at noon. Sometimes the wanting doesn't end when the package arrives; it moves on to the next thing. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, put a definition of wealth into one sentence. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: richness isn't having a great many things; real richness is richness of the soul.
screen: `A CART THAT NEVER CHECKS OUT.` → `THE WANTING MOVES ON.` → `RICHNESS OF THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: The word is qana'ah: contentment, being satisfied with what you've been given. The soul in the hadith is nafs, the same word this path has used for the self that wants and wants. So the hadith moves wealth off the shelf and into the self. Two people can own exactly the same things. One feels poor, because the wanting runs ahead. The other feels rich, because it doesn't. But qana'ah isn't a vow to have nothing. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says, in paraphrase: successful is the one who has submitted, been given enough to live on, and been made content by Allah with what He gave. Enough. Not nothing. A way to train it, also in Muslim, in paraphrase: look at those below you, not at those above you; that way you won't belittle Allah's blessings on you. Look down the ladder, not up. A phone feed tends to run the other way. And a story of someone who missed it. In surah al-Kahf, a man with two rich gardens walks into his own grounds and says he doesn't think any of this will ever perish. His companion asks him, in paraphrase: when you entered your garden, why didn't you say, what Allah wills; there is no strength except in Allah? Ma sha' Allah. You may hear it said over a new baby, a new house, a friend's success. It hands the good thing back to the One who gave it. Qana'ah is being able to stop at enough.
screen: `NAFS: WEALTH MOVES INTO THE SELF.` · `ENOUGH, NOT NOTHING.` · `LOOK DOWN THE LADDER, NOT UP.` · `THE TWO GARDENS: MA SHA' ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing you already own and haven't really looked at in a while, a mug, a coat, a window, shoes that still work, and look at it the way you'd look at something just unwrapped. Notice what it does for you every day without asking anything back. If you pray, you can say quietly, ma sha' Allah, or alhamdulillah; if not, just stay with the thing, and with the word enough.
Qana'ah. Contentment: richness of the soul, enough given and enough accepted, without the wanting running ahead. Today's word.
Your line: rich in the soul. Enough, not nothing. That's today, done.

1316.title: Excellence in all things
1316.hook: a blade being sharpened, and the odd place a hadith chose to talk about excellence
1316.howItsDone: Muslims learn ihsan from the hadith of Jibril, worshipping Allah as though you see Him, and apply the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws to everyday work, including slaughter with a sharp blade and without needless suffering.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qana'ah, rich in the soul. A week of virtues closes today, from pardon to contentment, with the one that runs underneath them all, first met as worship on day two hundred ninety-four.
screen: `RICH IN THE SOUL.` · `A WEEK OF VIRTUES.`

segments.voice: Where would you expect a teaching on excellence? A prayer hall, maybe, or a workshop. Not a blade being sharpened for an animal about to become a family's meal. But that's where the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, chose to put it. In Sahih Muslim, Shaddad ibn Aws reports him saying, in paraphrase: Allah has prescribed ihsan, excellence, in all things. So when you kill, kill well, and when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade and spare the animal suffering.
screen: `A BLADE BEING SHARPENED.` → `AN ODD PLACE FOR EXCELLENCE.` → `PRESCRIBED IN ALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Ihsan is doing a thing beautifully, doing it well. In the hadith of Jibril, in Sahih Muslim, it's described as worshipping Allah as though you see Him, and though you don't see Him, He sees you. Today's hadith carries it out of the prayer hall. First, the verb. The hadith says Allah kataba ihsan: wrote it, prescribed it, the same verb as in the fasting verse of al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's words: "Fasting is prescribed for you." So excellence isn't extra credit. It's written in. Second, the example. Of everything the hadith could have picked, it picks a moment where cutting corners costs someone who can't complain. Excellence here means care for the one with no voice: a sharp blade, no drawn-out pain. Third, the reach: in all things. If slaughter can be done with ihsan, so can a spreadsheet, a diaper change, an email, a pile of laundry. Ask who is on the other end of the task, and make it easier on them. Fourth, the week. Pardon done with ihsan doesn't keep a ledger. Justice done with ihsan is gentle. Ties kept with ihsan don't wait to be repaid. Loving for others with ihsan means the good, not just the polite. So ihsan isn't one more virtue on the list. It's the way every virtue gets done. Not perfection. Doing the thing well, because He sees.
screen: `AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.` · `KATABA: WRITTEN IN, NOT EXTRA.` · `CARE FOR THE ONE WITH NO VOICE.` · `HOW EVERY VIRTUE GETS DONE.`

segments.voice: Choose one ordinary task waiting for you, washing a pan, writing a reply, making the bed, and picture doing it well, not just fast: the right tool, your full attention, the last corner done. Then ask who will meet the result, and how it could be easier on them. If you pray, you can hold the hadith of Jibril in mind: as though you see Him, and He sees you.
Excellence in all things. Ihsan: doing each thing beautifully and well, prescribed, the hadith says, right down to a sharpened blade. Today's word.
Your line: excellence in everything. Written in, not extra credit. Tomorrow, the whole inward road at once.
